vignette:
Asha Patel is a 67-year-old South Asian American woman who has been married for decades and has spent much of her adult life working for a nonprofit organization, where she is known as steady, conscientious, and deeply committed to other people’s welfare. When she speaks about why she has come to treatment now, she does not begin with a list of symptoms. She begins with the assault itself, describing it in a careful, halting way that makes clear how present it still feels to her. The sexual assault happened in adulthood and left her with a sense that the world could change from ordinary to dangerous in an instant. What stays with her most is not only what was done to her, but the experience of being trapped inside it, unable to make it stop, and the humiliation of having her body treated as if it were no longer her own. Even now, when she recounts it, there are moments when she seems to lose her place in the room and speak as though it is happening again rather than as something that happened years ago.

In the weeks afterward, Asha tried to continue with her life in the way she believed she was supposed to. She went back to work at the nonprofit, answered emails, attended meetings, and told herself that keeping busy would be the most sensible thing. But the effort of appearing composed began to dominate her days. She found that reminders could arise without warning in very ordinary moments, and when they did she felt overwhelmed by the same fear, exposure, and bodily alarm she had known during the assault. At work, even moving through shared office space could feel loaded, because being in hallways, conference rooms, or doorways could suddenly make her feel cornered and intensely aware of who was near her. She became increasingly vigilant in her daily environment, scanning who was behind her, where the exits were, and how quickly she could leave if she needed to.

At home, her husband saw that she was no longer moving through the world with the ease she once had, though Asha struggled to explain it in a way that captured the force of her experience. What frightened her most was the sense that the assault had altered something fundamental about her safety and judgment. She had come to believe that the ordinary assumptions she once lived by—that she could read situations, that she could trust her surroundings, that she could protect herself—were no longer reliable. She did not describe this as an abstract belief; it showed up in dozens of small decisions. She avoided situations in which she might feel exposed, delayed errands, and became more cautious about being alone in settings that had previously felt unremarkable. If she could delegate a community visit, leave early, or rearrange her day to reduce uncertainty, she did.

Over months, these adjustments hardened into a narrower life. In her nonprofit role, where she had once welcomed in-person contact and community-facing work, she began structuring her responsibilities around what felt most manageable. Colleagues may have seen her as becoming more reserved or less available, but from Asha’s perspective she was trying to prevent the sudden surges of terror and vulnerability that could overtake her. The cost was that parts of her work, and parts of her marriage, became organized around what she could endure rather than what she wanted. She found herself less spontaneous with her husband, more guarded physically and emotionally, and then ashamed of that distance as well.

By the time she sought help, Asha was exhausted by the effort required to get through the day while carrying the assault so close to the surface. Her distress was severe, reflected in the intensity of what she reported, but in person it is conveyed less by dramatic display than by the relentless way the trauma intrudes on ordinary life. She speaks as someone who is tired of bracing herself. Coming to treatment seems to represent both necessity and risk for her. She wants relief from feeling as though danger is always one step away, and she wants some return of the steadiness that once defined her. At the same time, she is afraid that speaking about the assault in detail will bring her too close to it again, that she will be flooded by the same helplessness and violation she has spent so long trying to contain. Even so, what brings her in now is a quiet recognition that the life she has built—her marriage, her work, her sense of herself—has been increasingly constrained by what happened, and she does not want fear to keep deciding the terms of her days.
